study.title: Aleniglipron, a daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, in adults with obesity: a phase 2b randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

cover.headline: A GLP-1 you swallow took off 12.1% of body weight. **Placebo managed 0.5%.**

slides.title: The weight-loss drugs that work are injections. That is a real barrier for many people.
slides.body:
Semaglutide and tirzepatide changed obesity medicine, and both arrive as a weekly needle. Needles mean cold chain, prescriber training, and a hard no from a lot of patients.

A pill would dodge all of it. The problem is that the peptide drugs fall apart in the gut. So chemists have been hunting for a small molecule that hits the same receptor and survives being swallowed.

slides.title: Across 38 US sites, the top dose beat placebo by roughly twelve percentage points.
slides.body:
230 adults, average age 50, were randomly assigned to one of three doses or placebo for 36 weeks. Weight change came in at 9.0% on 45 mg, 10.7% on 90 mg and 12.1% on 120 mg, against 0.5% on placebo.

Gut side effects were mild to moderate and got less frequent as the trial ran on. About one in ten participants stopped early. No cases of drug-induced liver injury were reported.

stat.label: body weight lost on the top dose

caveats: The trial was funded by Structure Therapeutics, the company that owns the drug.
Phase 2b means 230 people over 36 weeks. Rare harms only show up in far larger trials.
Around one in ten quit before the end, so tolerability is not a solved problem.
Weight regain after stopping was not tested here. For every other GLP-1, it happens.

caption:
The interesting number here is not 12.1%. It is the 0.5% next to it.

This was a phase 2b randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of aleniglipron, a daily oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, in 230 adults with obesity across 38 US medical centres. At 36 weeks: 9.0% weight loss on 45 mg, 10.7% on 90 mg, 12.1% on 120 mg, and 0.5% on placebo. Gastrointestinal side effects were mild to moderate and eased over time. The discontinuation rate was 10.4%.

Two things to hold onto. The trial was funded by the company that owns the drug. And phase 2b is a signal, not a verdict.

Full study: doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04476-6

Pill or needle?
